Why Maryam Is Called the Sister of Aaron

Maryam's father was Imran and her mother Hanna. Vowed to the sanctuary before her birth, she was raised by Zakariyya, the husband of her sister, who won her charge by lot. Her Imran is not the Amram of the Torah, and sister of Aaron names kinship, not womb sisterhood. From the Ahl al-Bayt tafsir, al-Kafi, Lisan al-Arab, and the Gospel of Luke.
Article sections

When her people confront Maryam ﵍ with her infant, the Qur'an gives their address, the sister of Aaron, joined to a defense of her parents' honor (Qur'an 19:27-28). Aaron the prophet, brother of Moses ﵇, lived about a thousand years before her. Christian critics say the Qur'an has confused two women, Maryam ﵍ the mother of Isa ﵇ and Miriam the sister of Moses ﵇, and rolled them into one. If she was not Aaron's ﵇ sister, the charge concludes, the verse should never have said sister.

The surah's own story answers the family questions in order. Her father was Imran, and he is not the Amram who fathered Moses ﵇ and Aaron ﵇ a thousand years earlier; the two men share one ancient name, carried by the custom of naming children after the righteous. Sister of Aaron rides the same custom and the language's kinship grammar. The school's recorded readings, the Prophet's ﷺ own answer at Najran, the lexicons, the poetry they preserve, and the Gospel's kinship words all carry it.

The Imams ﵈, the twelve of the Ahl al-Bayt whom the school follows, read the verse this way from the beginning. Ali ibn Ibrahim al-Qummi (d.329 AH) narrates the scene and explains the address inside it. Al-Sharif al-Murtada (d.436) gave a session of his Amali to the readings of the verse. The objection reached the Prophet ﷺ in his own lifetime from the Christians of Najran, and his answer has chains in the Sunni and the Shia books alike.

Maryam's ﵍ father was Imran and her mother Hanna. In al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq ﵇ reports Allah's promise to Imran of a messenger son, and that Imran told his wife Hanna, she being the mother of Maryam. Al-Hilli (d.726) names the couple the same way (Idah al-Mukhalafa, p.204). The Qur'an opens her birth story with this woman's vow (Qur'an 3:35) and calls Maryam the daughter of Imran (Qur'an 66:12), naming the man of her own century.

She was vowed to the sanctuary, and Zakariyya ﵇, the husband of her sister, won her charge by lot. Her mother vowed the child as a muharrar, dedicated to the mosque for life. The custodians cast lots over her care, and the lot fell to Zakariyya, whom the school's report identifies as the husband of her sister (Nur al-Thaqalayn, vol.1, p.336). The Qur'an itself records the casting of the pens (Qur'an 3:44) and Zakariyya's charge (Qur'an 3:37). Guardianship by vow and lot leaves paternity where the Qur'an puts it, with Imran.

Her Imran is not the Amram of the Torah. The Torah's Amram fathered Aaron ﵇ and Moses ﵇ in the Exodus generation, a millennium and more before Maryam. Her father is the Imran of Zakariyya's century. The names are one name recurring, by the custom the Prophet ﷺ gave at Najran, that the Children of Israel named their children after their prophets and the righteous. The Bible never names Mary's father.

Sister of Aaron is a kinship address, and no reading in the surveyed record takes it for a womb sisterhood. The school's exegetes recorded the readings. A righteous namesake of her own people, with the Najran answer behind it. A woman of Aaron's ﵇ line, stated by al-Murtada among the readings and glossed by Muqatil at the verse. A wicked namesake the crowd reached for as an insult, in al-Qummi's narration. A righteous brother who shared neither of her parents. On none of them does the verse name a womb-sister of Moses' ﵇ brother, and that is the only reading the confusion charge needs.

No recorded reading makes the verse name a womb-sister of Aaron the prophet. From Premise 1 and Premise 2, the family is fixed. Her father Imran, her mother Hanna, her guardian the husband of her sister, chosen by the sanctuary's lot. From Premise 3, the father is a man of her own century whose ancient name the custom explains. From Premise 4, the address carries kinship in the language's own grammar, the Imams' ﵈ usage, the lexicons, the poetry they preserve, and the Gospel's kinship words. The charge needs sister to mean one womb, and no part of the evidence gives it that rule.

Her Father Was Imran
The Qur'an names her parents through her own story. Her father was a man named Imran, her mother Hanna. The school's reports state the couple directly.
Source: al-Kafi, vol.1, p.583, narration 1
Speaker: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq ﵇
Locus: Allah's promise to Imran, told to his wife Hanna
Claim: Maryam's ﵍ parents are Imran and Hanna

Al-Hilli (d.726) names the couple the same way, the wife of Imran being Hanna, the mother of Maryam daughter of Imran, mother of the Messiah (Idah al-Mukhalafa, p.204). The promise of a messenger son thus ran through her, and the son it meant was Isa ﵇ himself.
Verse: Qur'an 3:35, Surat Al Imran
Claim: the wife of Imran, her mother, dedicates the child she carries
The woman making the vow is her mother, and the Imran of the vow is her father. When the Qur'an calls Maryam ﵍ the daughter of Imran (Qur'an 66:12), it names this man.
Verse: Qur'an 66:12, Surat al-Tahrim
Claim: daughter names her actual father, Imran, husband of Hanna
Claim: her father carried the ancient name of the House of Imran
Daughter here is literal paternity, a man of her own century, the husband of Hanna. The charge never disputes this verse.
Zakariyya, the Husband of Her Sister, Won Her Charge by Lot
Her mother vowed the child in her womb as a muharrar, dedicated to the mosque's service for life. A vowed child belonged to the sanctuary, and the men drew lots for her care.
Source: al-Huwayzi (d.1112 AH), Nur al-Thaqalayn, vol.1, p.336, from al-Ayyashi, from Ismail al-Jufi
Speaker: Imam Muhammad al-Baqir ﵇
Locus: the vow of the wife of Imran and the lots over Maryam's ﵍ charge
Claim: Zakariyya ﵇ won the lot and was the husband of her sister

The report of Imam al-Baqir ﵇ adds the fact the Qur'an does not spell out. Zakariyya ﵇ was the husband of her sister, her own kin, and her charge fell to him when his lot won. The Qur'an itself records the casting.

Source: al-Burhan fi Tafsir al-Qur'an, vol.1, p.684, report 1701

The vow had made her the sanctuary's child, so the sanctuary's men drew for her.
Verse: Qur'an 3:37 (part)
Claim: Zakariyya takes charge of her in the prayer-niche
Source: al-Kafi, vol.3, p.109
Speaker: Imam al-Baqir
Claim: the prophets cast lots for her charge
Her Imran Is Not the Amram of the Torah
Verse: Exodus 6:20
Source: Westminster Leningrad Codex,King James Version
Claim: Amram's children are Aaron ﵇ and Moses ﵇

Amram's children are Aaron ﵇ and Moses ﵇, and Maryam's ﵍ own father carried the same name, Imran, the husband of Hanna. They are two different men, a millennium apart. The shared name is the custom the Prophet ﷺ gave as his answer at Najran, that the Children of Israel named their children after their prophets and the righteous before them. The Bible never names Mary's father at all; the Qur'an names him, and names him a man of her own time.
Verse: Qur'an 3:33-34, Surat Aal Imran
Claim: the chosen houses bound into one seed
Claim: Maryam's ﵍ house is a link in the chosen line

The third surah carries the house's name in its own title, Al Imran, and binds that house into the chain of chosen houses, one seed from one another. That is her family, the house of her father Imran and her mother Hanna, not the Exodus generation. The school reads her election, Allah has chosen you above the women of the worlds (Qur'an 3:42), as election into that lineage.
What Sister of Aaron Means
When Maryam ﵍ returned carrying the infant, her people met her with the address, and the charge reads it as a confusion of two women.
The crowd's charge comes first. The address and the parentage defense follow inside one speech.
Verse: Qur'an 19:27-28, Surat Maryam
Locus: Maryam ﵍ returns to her people carrying the infant Isa ﵇
Speaker: the assembly of the Children of Israel, with Zakariyya ﵇ present in Tafsir al-Qummi's narration
Claim: the crowd invokes her lineage's honor while charging her with a thing unheard of
Source: Musnad Ahmad (al-Risala ed.), vol.30, p.141; also Ibn Asakir, Tarikh Dimashq, vol.70, p.98, no.13795; Sahih Muslim, Kitab al-Adab
Speaker: al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, the envoy to Najran
Claim: the objection was raised in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime and answered by him
Source: Ibn Tawus (d.664 AH), Sa'd al-Su'ud, from al-Azdi, from Simak ibn Harb, in Nur al-Thaqalayn, vol.3, p.333
Chain: a Shia transmission of the same event
Claim: the school keeps the Najran exchange in its own books

The report attests that the verse was heard and tested within the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime by Christians who knew the scriptures the charge draws on. It also preserves the answer in the Prophet's own words. The Children of Israel used to attach their children to their prophets and righteous men, and an address by a saint's name follows that custom. The same report stands in Sahih Muslim's Kitab al-Adab, among the most strictly graded Sunni collections. The records of the exchange in both communities' books carry it from al-Mughira.

Al-Murtada's Amali keeps the exchange in the school's own sitting, where the Prophet's ﷺ rebuke is softened into a lesson (Amali, vol.2, p.197). Al-Mughira was silent on the spot, and the answer he carried back named a custom checkable in the objectors' own scripture.
Source: al-Sharif al-Murtada (d.436 AH), Amali (Ghurar al-Fawa'id), session 68, vol.2, p.197
Open question: what sister of Aaron means
Claim: the address names a woman of Aaron's ﵇ line the way an Arab is named by his tribe

Al-Murtada states the reading with the tribe parallel in his own hand, sister of Aaron read as a woman of the line, addressed the way an Arab is addressed by his tribe. He records it among the readings without closing the session on it alone. The idiom was ordinary Arabic to a first-rank scholar of the school.
Source: Muqatil ibn Sulayman (d.150 AH), in al-Murtada, Amali, vol.2, p.197
Source: from the Prophet ﷺ
Claim: this Aaron is Aaron the brother of Moses ﵇, and the address means one of his line

The report grants the charge its identification. The Aaron of the address is Aaron the prophet ﵇, brother of Moses ﵇, and that much is what the Prophet's ﷺ report gives. The lineage gloss is Muqatil's own, that brother-of in the Qur'an's mouth means one of their descendants and their kind, exactly the Hud and Salih construction he cites.

Muqatil's standing is the obvious objection. He is an early transmitter whom the later critics graded harshly, and a hostile reader will say so; the school's case does not lean on him. Al-Murtada, the hardest critic of reports his generation produced, cites him as one reading among several. Every other reading carries the same conclusion from other evidence, through the Qur'an's own usage, the naming custom from Najran, the lexicons, and the living speech. If Muqatil fails as a witness, the idiom still rests on that evidence; if he holds, he carries the report that names the Aaron of the address.
Source: al-Sharif al-Murtada, Amali, vol.4, p.106, from the early exegetes
Claim: a righteous Harun of her people
Claim: forty thousand men named Harun followed his funeral

Forty thousand men named Harun at one funeral is a report's way of saying the name filled the city. Behind the number stands a people who named their sons after the saints of the line so consistently that a righteous Harun could die with a crowd of his namesakes behind his bier. A woman of that people, addressed by the same name, is being measured against the house's standard of piety.
Source: Ali ibn Ibrahim al-Qummi (d.329 AH), Tafsir al-Qummi, vol.2, p.50
Reports: the school's inherited account of the birth scene of Isa ﵇
Claim: the crowd likened her to a wicked man named Harun of their own time

On this reading the crowd named no genealogy of hers. They cut her with a comparison to a notorious man of their own generation, a Harun known for sin. The address is an insult, and an insult needs a reference the audience shares. A Harun of their own day gives them one, and the verse reports their words without endorsing their sneer. On this reading too, the thousand years the confusion charge needs are gone, since a contemporary Harun stands inside Maryam's ﵍ own world. Al-Qummi's Harun is a wicked man and the exegetes' Harun is a saint, and the disagreement between the reports is real. The two readings still share one presupposition, that the name Harun sat on many men of her people, and that breadth of the name is what the naming custom rests on. A name forty thousand men carried sat on sinners and saints alike, and a crowd reaching for the house's name could reach for a notorious namesake or a holy one. The two readings answer different questions, al-Qummi's namesake telling which man the crowd reached for, and the lineage readings telling whose house the name carries.

Later compilations gather the collected readings, and the Sunni exegetical tradition carries the same range. Al-Farra (d.207), the founder of the Kufan school of Qur'anic grammar, keeps a brother in the picture, one who shares neither of her parents.
Source: al-Huwayzi (d.1112 AH), Nur al-Thaqalayn, vol.3, p.333
Claim: the collected views on sister of Aaron, from Ibn Abbas to al-Mughira
Source: al-Farra (d.207 AH), Ma'ani al-Qur'an, vol.2, p.167
Claim: a brother who does not share her parents
In the earliest recorded readings the kinship word already named lineage and stock, with no shared womb in question.

No recorded reading takes the sister of the address for a womb-sister of the brother of Moses ﵇, and that is the only reading the confusion charge needs. The conclusion is narrower than the polemic and sufficient for the verse. On the Gospel's own kinship words Maryam's ﵍ kin are of the house of Aaron ﵇. Direct descent from Aaron is a recorded reading, plausible without being textually demonstrated. The address itself needs only the kinship grammar of Arabic and the scriptures' own kinship words.
Her Kin in the Bible
The Gospel agrees that the guardian's household was her own family, and it joins that family to the house of Aaron.
Verse: Luke 1:5
Source: Elzevir Textus Receptus,King James Version
Claim: Elizabeth is of the daughters of Aaron
Verse: Luke 1:36
Source: Elzevir Textus Receptus,King James Version
Claim: Elizabeth is Maryam's kinswoman

Luke makes Zakariyya ﵇ a priest of the temple divisions and his wife Elizabeth a woman of the daughters of Aaron, and calls Elizabeth Maryam's ﵍ kinswoman, syngenis, a relative. The school's report that Zakariyya was the husband of her sister meets the Gospel on the same ground. The guardian was family, and the family ran into the house of Aaron. The Gospel does not state that Maryam ﵍ herself descended from Aaron; the kinship can run through the mothers.
The school saw the Luke chain a century ago and committed it to print in a book of answers to Christian mission.
Source: Muhammad Jawad al-Balaghi (d.1352 AH), al-Rihla al-Madrasiyya, vol.1, p.175
Claim: al-Balaghi's inference from Luke's first chapter makes Maryam's ﵍ line Aaronic

Al-Balaghi presses the inference at its strongest, that the shared lineage runs whole and Maryam ﵍ is paternally Aaronic. The Gospel itself says less, and that much is certain. It makes Maryam ﵍ a blood relative of a woman of Aaron's house. Which line the shared blood runs through, father's or mother's, the tradition itself divides, and John of Damascus (d.749) draws the maternal Aaronic line in his Homily on the Nativity, Joachim of Judah and David for her father's side, an Aaronic, Levitical house for her mother's. The tradition that presses the charge carries, in its own memory, the Aaronic kin the address names.
Source: Ibn al-Athir (d.630 AH), al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, vol.1, p.327
Claim: Maryam ﵍ was of Judah and David, and the address rides the naming custom

The counter-branch itself concedes the custom. Ibn al-Athir grants that she was of the line of Aaron, so it has been said. He then explains the address by the naming custom, they were called after the righteous, which is the Prophet's ﷺ own answer from Najran. One branch of the tradition holds her of Aaron's ﵇ blood, with sisterhood naming the line. The other holds her of Judah, with the address following the naming custom. A third branch, on which the crowd's words claim a womb shared with the brother of Moses ﵇, appears nowhere in the surveyed readings.
Verse: Mark 6:3
Source: Elzevir Textus Receptus,King James Version
Claim: the Lord's kin are named with the brother-word

The Greek adelphos holds the same breadth the Hebrew ach carried into it, and the word names the kin around the Lord. The long argument inside Christianity over these brothers is an argument from context, because the word itself carries both kin and sibling.
Verse: Genesis 13:8
Source: Westminster Leningrad Codex,King James Version
Claim: Abraham and Lot called brethren, uncle and nephew
Verse: Numbers 20:14
Source: Westminster Leningrad Codex,King James Version
Claim: Israel named the brother nation of Edom

Abraham says to Lot, we be brethren, and Lot is his nephew, so the brother-word covers a named man who shares no womb with Abraham. These verses carry the form the surveyed Arabic record does not attest separately, a kinship word joined to one named individual. The Hebrew ach carries kinsman as easily as brother, and the Gospel's Greek inherits the breadth. The assembly that confronted Maryam ﵍ spoke that Hebrew or its Aramaic daughter, and the Qur'an recites their address in Arabic. The objection that seventh-century Arabic cannot tell what first-century Israelites meant is answered from the charge's own scriptures, which carry the same wide kinship field in the crowd's own language.

The Torah's history uses the same words for nations a thousand years apart. Moses ﵇ writes to Edom centuries after Esau and names Israel the brother nation, the two brothers Jacob and Esau standing at the head of both lines. A descendant people is a brother people, generation after generation, in the very scriptures the charge appeals to.

The woman's name is Maryam, Miriam, the name of Aaron's ﵇ own sister, borne inside the house of Aaron by the custom of naming after the righteous that the Prophet ﷺ gave as his answer at Najran. The Torah, when it honors Miriam the prophetess, titles her the sister of Aaron ﵇.
Verse: Exodus 15:20
Source: Westminster Leningrad Codex,King James Version
Claim: the Torah itself titles Miriam the sister of Aaron

A hostile reader may hand this verse to the charge instead, since Miriam truly was Aaron's ﵇ sister by the womb. Miriam is Moses' ﵇ sister too, and the Torah titles her by the house's priest, the sister of Aaron ﵇, the ascription that carries the house's honor. A woman who could have been named by the more famous brother is named by the one whose line carried the priesthood, and the crowd's address makes the same choice a thousand years later. The title the Torah gives the first woman of that name is the address the crowd gave Maryam ﵍.
The Address in the Language

Contested words. The charge reads ukht, sister, as one born of the same parents only. The Imams' ﵈ own usage, the lexicons, and the poetry they preserve fix the word as kinship within a house, covering descendants and tribesmen.
Verse: Qur'an 7:65 (part)
Claim: a prophet of the stock of Ad is called the nation's brother
Verse: Qur'an 7:73 (part)
Claim: a prophet of the stock of Thamud likewise

Hud shares no womb with the whole nation Ad, and Salih shares none with every man of Thamud. The Qur'an sends Shu'ayb to Madyan in the same register (Qur'an 7:85). It calls each prophet the brother of the nation he was sent to because he is of their stock and their kind.

Daughter of Imran shows the kinship word joined to a named individual, for descent. Brother of Ad and brother of Thamud show the kinship word joined to a collective, for belonging. What 19:28 writes, a feminine kinship word joined to the house's named saint, composes those two registers. No independent Arabic example of this exact form, a kinship word joined to one named man, survives in the surveyed record. The two registers are each attested, and the verse's own early exegetes read the composition without strain, Muqatil glossing it at the verse itself and al-Murtada stating it with the Tamim parallel. The Qur'an spends the same words more loosely still. It calls the believers brothers wherever they live (Qur'an 49:10), and the reckless spendthrifts brothers of the devils (Qur'an 17:27), where no blood is in question.

In al-Kafi, a woman named Juwayra is waiting in the Sacred Mosque for a mawla of her family, a freed slave attached to the household. Imam al-Sadiq ﵇ asks her what she is waiting for, and when he learns the man was never freed himself, only his grandfather was, he corrects her word for the relationship.
Source: al-Kafi, vol.6, p.199, narration 4
Speaker: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq ﵇
Locus: Juwayra waits for a mawla of the family in the Sacred Mosque
Claim: the grandson of the freed dependent is called your brother

The Imam ﵇ names the grandson of the freed dependent a brother of the house, inside a ruling on clientage (wala'), and no transmitter in the report questions the word. Akh, brother, in the mouth of the school covers kinship across generations.

A man of Tamim came to Umar asking for a share of water in a land grant, and al-Zubayr addressed him by his tribe. Ibn Manzur (d.711) preserves the exchange in Lisan al-Arab, the largest classical dictionary of the language, and al-Azhari (d.370) had carried the same scene three centuries earlier in Tahdhib al-Lugha. The two lexicons quote the scene under their entry for shibak, a dense cluster of wells, and they preserve the address as ordinary speech.
Source: Ibn Manzur, Lisan al-Arab, vol.10, p.447
Speaker: al-Zubayr, before Umar
Dating: the scene from the first century AH, carried by Ibn Manzur (d.711 AH)
Claim: a man of Tamim is addressed as the brother of Tamim
Source: al-Azhari, Tahdhib al-Lugha, vol.10, p.20
Speaker: al-Zubayr, before Umar
Dating: al-Azhari (d.370 AH)
Claim: the same scene and vocative three centuries earlier

Two dictionaries, three centuries apart, cite the same vocative because it was the living idiom of the address. Tamim is a tribe, an ancestor's name carried by a whole people, and the man of that stock is greeted by it. The Imam's ﵇ correction and the lexicons' scene attest the same address independently.

The dictionary carries a poet's line in its own pages, a pre-Islamic taunt addressed to a man of Banu Khalaf by his clan's name. The taunt's grammar is the grammar of the 19:28 scene, an address by the house's name in the middle of a rebuke.
Source: a pre-Islamic poet, in Lisan al-Arab, vol.11, p.740
Claim: a man of Banu Khalaf is addressed as their brother

The lexicons record the address as ordinary grammar, and the poet opens a taunt with it. Zibriqan hears his clan's name from a man insulting him, and the insult needs no gloss to be understood. Speakers used the address before any dictionary recorded it, and al-Murtada's session on 19:28 explains the verse with this exact form.

In the longest case, an Egyptian skeptic, a zindiq, a denier of prophethood, traveled to Makkah to argue with Imam al-Sadiq ﵇ and found him in the tawaf, the ritual walk around the Kaaba. The Imam ﵇ answered him question by question, and at every turn he addressed the man by his city.
Source: al-Kafi (Dar al-Hadith ed.), vol.1, pp.423-425
Speaker: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq ﵇
Locus: the Egyptian zindiq debates the Imam ﵇ during the tawaf
Claim: a total stranger is addressed as the brother of the people of Egypt

The Imam ﵇ had never seen this man before the man laid a hand on his shoulder mid-tawaf. The address names the stranger by his people, brother of the people of Egypt, and the debate ran on with the address repeated down the page. The vocative, the grammar of calling, carries a kinship word and a people's name together as easily as an English speaker says a name alone. The Najran objection, put to the Prophet's ﷺ envoy a century and a half before this debate and told under What Sister of Aaron Means, concerned the thousand years between Moses and Jesus, never the Arabic of the address.

The Canon Does Not Pass Its Own Test
Source: the Gospels of Matthew, Luke, and Mark; Helvidius (4th c.); Jerome, Against Helvidius (383); John of Damascus, Homily on the Nativity (8th c.)
Claim: Mary's Davidic line; the Aaronic line of her kinswoman; the perpetual virginity and the brothers of the Lord
Open question: does the Christian canon survive the test it presses on Qur'an 19:28

The charge's rule, that a kinship word means the womb, is the polemicists' own. The Christian canon meets it on the four measures this confusion charge must answer, fidelity to the text, coherence, the ethical cost, and economy.

Christian tradition traces the Lord's family to David, and Matthew opens his Gospel with the claim. Luke builds the Aaronic link into the infancy narrative through Elizabeth, as shown above. Helvidius, writing at Rome before 383, taught that the brothers named in Mark 6:3 were the Virgin's own sons by Joseph, and Jerome reports him so. Jerome answered that they were kin, the sons of Mary the wife of Alphaeus, called Mary of Clopas. He takes her for the sister or kinswoman of the Lord's mother, so that sons of the mother's sister can be called the Lord's brethren (Jerome, Against Helvidius, 383, chs. 14-16). The older tradition holds the Virgin ever virgin, a title the Second Council of Constantinople confessed in 553. John of Damascus (d.749) gives Mary a double lineage in his Homily on the Nativity, Davidic on her father's side, Aaronic on her mother's. The canon's own family register thus runs through the same wide kinship words, and the strongest Christian readings of them are readings of kinship. The kinship words carry the range the charge denies to Arabic.
Verse: Matthew 1:1
Source: Elzevir Textus Receptus,King James Version
Claim: the Gospel opens the Lord's genealogy with the son of David

Son of David is son a thousand years after David, and no Christian tradition has read it as a literal paternity. The canon's own opening verse runs on the genealogical kinship grammar that the charge refuses to Arabic.

On textual fidelity, the Islamic reading keeps every word of 19:28 in its attested range. Ukht stays house-kinship, Aaron stays the house's saint, and the parentage defense stays the address's own frame. The charge must read one kinship word of one book literally. The same book calls a nation the sons of a patriarch a millennium dead and two prophets the brothers of whole nations, and the charge offers no rule that separates them. Its own Numbers joins a kinship word to one named individual, Israel, for a descendant people (Numbers 20:14).

On rational coherence, the charge's rule fails inside the Christian canon itself. Brethren names a nephew in Genesis, a brother nation in Numbers, and the Lord's kin in Mark. A Christian who accepts his own canon's usage has no coherent ground to deny the same range to Arabic. A Christian may answer that his canon is human report while the Qur'an claims to be God's own word, so a blunder in it would be fatal. The answer does not rescue the rule. The charge's claim is about what the Arabic word sister can mean, and that is a fact of the language, whoever is speaking.

On the ethical criterion, the charge asks a reader to believe that the book of God blundered in a genealogy plain on a first reading. The reading asks only that God spoke the kinship grammar the language's speakers, lexicons, and poets actually used, and that the first objectors were answered from the source in the verse's own lifetime.

On economy, the reading needs one settled idiom to carry every exhibit above, while the charge needs a confusion no surveyed transmitter reports, an idiom no dictionary supports, and a rule the canon itself breaks.

The canon that reads son of David across a millennium and brethren across a family network cannot rule that sister across a house is a blunder. The Christian who declines the test, reading his own kinship words by context, has granted the whole method.
Final Verdict

The charge requires the verse to name a womb-sister of Aaron the prophet, and no reading in the surveyed record does. Her father was Imran and her mother Hanna. Her mother vowed her to the sanctuary, and Zakariyya ﵇, the husband of her sister, won her charge by lot. Her Imran is a man of her own century, not the Amram of the Torah. The two share one name by the custom the Prophet ﷺ gave at Najran, where this objection was first raised and answered by him in his own lifetime. The school's readings give the address a righteous namesake or a house's lineage. The descendant reading is recorded without being established, and the Gospel itself joins Maryam's ﵍ kin to the daughters of Aaron while never calling her Aaron's ﵇ descendant. The language settles what the genealogy leaves open. Kinship words in Arabic, in Hebrew, and in the Qur'an itself name houses and lines, and sister of Aaron is that address.

The canon that presses the literal reading does not carry it at home. Son of David opens its first Gospel, brethren names a nephew in Genesis and a nation in Numbers, and the Lord's own brothers at Nazareth are read by context even inside Christianity. A scripture whose kinship words are read by context has no ground to deny the same reading to another scripture's sister-word. The verse said sister because sister was true, in the language it was said in, to the woman of Aaron's ﵇ house standing before the assembly with her son in her arms.
Glossary
ukht sister, the feminine of akh, brother. The Arabic kinship words cover descendants and tribesmen of a house, and the address grammar joins them to a people's name.
aal the house or line of a father, as in Aal Imran, the House of Imran, the third surah's title.
mawla a freed slave or client attached to a household, with a bond of patronage the Arabs counted as a form of kinship.
zindiq a skeptic who denies prophethood, the Egyptian debater of al-Kafi.
vocative the grammar of calling, the case that addresses a person directly, ya before the name in Arabic.
honorific marks the small characters after sacred names, ﷺ for the Prophet Muhammad, ﵇ for male saints and Imams, ﵍ for female saints, ﵈ for the Imams together, abbreviating blessings upon them.

"She had a brother named Aaron, one of the best of the Children of Israel, though he was not from her two parents. So it was said, 'sister of Aaron,' for his righteousness. Your brother is righteous, and your parents are your parents."

quotes.caption: The Gospel of Luke 1:5; Greek, Elzevir Textus Receptus; English, King James Version

paragraphs.text: εγενετο εν ταις ημεραις ηρωδου του βασιλεως της ιουδαιας ιερευς τις ονοματι ζαχαριας εξ εφημεριας αβια και η γυνη αυτου εκ των θυγατερων ααρων και το ονομα αυτης ελισαβετ
Egeneto en tais hēmerais Hērōdou tou basileōs tēs Ioudaias hiereus tis onomati Zacharias ex ephēmerias Abia, kai hē gunē autou ek tōn thugaterōn Aarōn, kai to onoma autēs Elisabet
"There was in the days of Herod, the king of Judaea, a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abia; and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elisabeth."

quotes.caption: The Gospel of Luke 1:36; Greek, Elzevir Textus Receptus; English, King James Version

paragraphs.text: και ιδου ελισαβετ η συγγενης σου και αυτη συνειληφυια υιον εν γηρα αυτης και ουτος μην εκτος εστιν αυτη τη καλουμενη στειρα
kai idou Elisabet hē syngenēs sou kai autē syneilēphyia huion en gēra autēs, kai houtos mēn hektos estin autē tē kaloumenē steira
"And, behold, thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month with her, who was called barren."

quotes.caption: Muhammad Jawad al-Balaghi, al-Rihla al-Madrasiyya, vol.1, p.175

paragraphs.text: والذي يستنتج من الفصل الأول من إنجيل لوقا هو أن تكون مريم من نسل هارون من سبط ( لاوي ) لا من نسل داود من سبط يهوذا .
فإنه يصرح في العدد الخامس بأن اليصابات زوجة زكريا هي من نسل هارون . ويصرح في العدد السادس والثلاثين بأن اليصابات نسيبة مريم فإن مشاركتها في النسب تقتضي أن تكون مريم من بنات هارون أي نسبا
"What follows from the first chapter of the Gospel of Luke is that Maryam was of the line of Aaron, of the tribe of Levi, not of the line of David, of the tribe of Judah."

"It states in verse five that Elizabeth, the wife of Zakariyya, was of the line of Aaron, and it states in verse thirty-six that Elizabeth was a relative of Maryam. Her sharing in the lineage requires that Maryam be of the daughters of Aaron, by lineage."

quotes.caption: Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh, vol.1, p.327

paragraphs.text: وكانت من نسل هارون أخي موسى ، كذا قيل [ 2 ] . قلت : إنّها ليست من نسل هارون إنّما هي من سبط يهوذا بن يعقوب من نسل سليمان بن داود ، وإنّما كانوا يدعون بالصالحين ، وهارون من ولد لاوي بن يعقوب

"She was of the line of Aaron the brother of Moses, so it has been said. I say, she was not of the line of Aaron; she was of the tribe of Judah son of Jacob, of the line of Solomon son of David. Rather, they were called after the righteous, and Aaron was of the descendants of Levi son of Jacob."

quotes.caption: The Gospel of Mark 6:3; Greek, Elzevir Textus Receptus; English, King James Version

paragraphs.text: ουχ ουτος εστιν ο τεκτων ο υιος μαριας αδελφος δε ιακωβου και ιωση και ιουδα και σιμωνος και ουκ εισιν αι αδελφαι αυτου ωδε προς ημας και εσκανδαλιζοντο εν αυτω
ouch houtos estin ho tektōn ho huios Marias, adelphos de Iakōbou kai Iōsē kai Iouda kai Simōnos, kai ouk eisin hai adelphai autou hōde pros hēmas kai eskandalizonto en autō
"Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon? and are not his sisters here with us? And they were offended at him."

quotes.caption: The Torah, Genesis 13:8; Hebrew, Westminster Leningrad Codex; English, King James Version

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אַבְרָ֜ם אֶל־לֹ֗וט אַל־נָ֨א תְהִ֤י מְרִיבָה֙ בֵּינִ֣י וּבֵינֶ֔יךָ וּבֵ֥ין רֹעַ֖י וּבֵ֣ין רֹעֶ֑יךָ כִּֽי־אֲנָשִׁ֥ים אַחִ֖ים אֲנָֽחְנוּ׃
vayyōmer Avram el-Lôṭ, al-nā tehî merîvāh bênî ûḇênêḵā ûḇên roʿay ûḇên roʿêḵā, kî-anāšîm aḥîm anaḥnû
"And Abram said unto Lot, Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we be brethren."

quotes.caption: The Torah, Numbers 20:14; Hebrew, Westminster Leningrad Codex; English, King James Version

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׁלַ֨ח מֹשֶׁ֧ה מַלְאָכִ֛ים מִקָּדֵ֖שׁ אֶל־מֶ֣לֶךְ אֱדֹ֑ום כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ אָחִ֣יךָ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אַתָּ֣ה יָדַ֔עְתָּ אֵ֥ת כָּל־הַתְּלָאָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר מְצָאָֽתְנוּ׃
vayyišlaḥ Môšeh malʾāḵîm miqqādeš el-meleḵ ʾEdôm, kôh ʾāmar ʾaḥîḵā Yiśrāʾēl, ʾattāh yāḏaʿtā ʾet kol-hattəlāʾāh ʾašer məṣāʾtēnû
"And Moses sent messengers from Kadesh unto the king of Edom, Thus saith thy brother Israel, Thou knowest all the travail that hath befallen us."

quotes.caption: The Torah, Exodus 15:20; Hebrew, Westminster Leningrad Codex; English, King James Version

paragraphs.text: וַתִּקַּח֩ מִרְיָ֨ם הַנְּבִיאָ֜ה אֲחֹ֧ות אַהֲרֹ֛ן אֶת־הַתֹּ֖ף בְּיָדָ֑הּ וַתֵּצֶ֤אןָ כָֽל־הַנָּשִׁים֙ אַחֲרֶ֔יהָ בְּתֻפִּ֖ים וּבִמְחֹלֹֽת׃
vattiqqaḥ Miryām hanneḇîʾāh aḥôt Ahărôn et-hattôp beyādāh, vattēṣeʾnā kol-hannāšîm aḥāreyhā batuppîm ūḇimḥōlōt
"And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances."

quotes.caption: Qur'an 7:65 (part)

paragraphs.text: وَإِلَىٰ عَادٍ أَخَاهُمْ هُودًۭا
wa-ilā ʿĀdin akhāhum Hūdā
"And to Ad, their brother Hud."

quotes.caption: Qur'an 7:73 (part)

paragraphs.text: وَإِلَىٰ ثَمُودَ أَخَاهُمْ صَٰلِحًۭا
wa-ilā Thamūda akhāhum Ṣāliḥā
"And to Thamud, their brother Salih."

quotes.caption: Imam al-Sadiq, al-Kulayni, al-Kafi, vol.6, p.199

paragraphs.text: مر بي أبو عبد الله ﵇ وأنا في المسجد الحرام أنتظر مولى لنا فقال : يا أم عثمان ما يقيمك ههنا ؟
فقلت : أنتظر مولى لنا ، فقال : أعتقتموه ؟ فقلت : لا ، فقال : أعتقتم أباه ؟ قلت : لا ، أعتقنا جده ، فقال : ليس هذا مولاكم بل هذا أخوكم
"Abu Abd Allah passed by me while I was in the Sacred Mosque waiting for a dependent of ours. He said, 'Umm Uthman, what keeps you here?'"

"I said, 'I am waiting for a dependent of ours.' He said, 'Did you free him?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'Did you free his father?' I said, 'No, we freed his grandfather.' He said, 'He is not your dependent. He is your brother.'"

quotes.caption: Ibn Manzur, Lisan al-Arab, vol.10, p.447

paragraphs.text: فقال الزبير : إنك يا أخا تميم تسأل خيراً قليلًا ، فقال عمر ، ﵁ : لا بل خير كثير قِرْبَتانِ قِرْبةٌ من ماء وقربة من لبن
"Al-Zubayr said, 'You, O brother of Tamim, ask for little good.' Umar said, 'No, for much good, two skins, a skin of water and a skin of milk.'"

quotes.caption: Al-Azhari, Tahdhib al-Lugha, vol.10, p.20

paragraphs.text: فقال الزبير : إنك يا أخا تميم تسأل خيراً قليلًا فقال عمر : لا بل خير كثيرٌ ، قِرْبتانِ ، قربةٌ من ماء ، وقربة من لبَن
"Al-Zubayr said, 'You, O brother of Tamim, ask for little good.' Umar said, 'No, for much good, two skins, a skin of water and a skin of milk.'"

quotes.caption: The poet's taunt, in Ibn Manzur, Lisan al-Arab, vol.11, p.740

paragraphs.text: يا زِبْرِقان ، أَخا بني خَلَفٍ ، * ما أَنت ، وَيْبَ أَبيك والفَخْر
"O Zibriqan, brother of the sons of Khalaf, what has come over you, fie upon your father, and this boasting?"

quotes.caption: Imam al-Sadiq, al-Kafi (Dar al-Hadith ed.), vol.1, pp.423-425

paragraphs.text: قَالَ لِي هِشَامُ بْنُ الْحَكَمِ : كَانَ بِمِصْرَ زِنْدِيقٌ (3) يَبْلُغُهُ (4) عَنْ أَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ ﵇ أَشْيَاءُ ، فَخَرَجَ إِلَى الْمَدِينَةِ لِيُنَاظِرَهُ ، فَلَمْ يُصَادِفْهُ بِهَا ، وَقِيلَ لَهُ : إِنَّهُ خَارِجٌ بِمَكَّةَ ،

فَخَرَجَ إِلى مَكَّةَ وَنَحْنُ مَعَ أَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ ﵇ (5) ، فَصَادَفَنَا وَنَحْنُ مَعَ أَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ ﵇ فِي الطَّوَافِ ، وَكَانَ اسْمَهُ عَبْدُ الْمَلِكِ ، وَكُنْيَتَهُ أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ ،
فَضَرَبَ كَتِفَهُ كَتِفَ أَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ ﵇ ، فَقَالَ لَهُ

فَقَالَ أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ ﵇ : « أَيُّهَا الرَّجُلُ ، لَيْسَ لِمَنْ لَايَعْلَمُ حُجَّةٌ عَلى مَنْ يَعْلَمُ ، وَلا حُجَّةَ لِلْجَاهِلِ (7) ، يَا أَخَا أَهْلِ مِصْرَ ، تَفَهَّمْ عَنِّي (8) ؛ فَإِنَّا لَانَشُكُّ فِي اللَّهِ أَبَداً ،

أَمَا تَرَى الشَّمْسَ وَالْقَمَرَ ، وَاللَّيْلَ وَالنَّهَارَ يَلِجَانِ (9) فَلَا (10) يَشْتَبِهَانِ (11) ، وَيَرْجِعَانِ قَدِ اضْطُرَّا ، لَيْسَ لَهُمَا مَكَانٌ إِلَّا مَكَانُهُمَا ، فَإِنْ كَانَا يَقْدِرَانِ عَلى أَنْ يَذْهَبَا ، فَلِمَ يَرْجِعَانِ ؟
"Hisham ibn al-Hakam said to me, 'There was in Egypt a zindiq to whom reports about Abu Abd Allah reached. He went to Madina to debate with him, but did not find him there."
"He was told that he had gone out to Makkah, so he went to Makkah while we were with Abu Abd Allah. He encountered us while we were with Abu Abd Allah in the tawaf."
"His name was Abd al-Malik, and his kunya was Abu Abd Allah. He struck his shoulder against the shoulder of Abu Abd Allah.'"
"Imam al-Sadiq said, 'Man, one who does not know has no argument against one who knows, and the ignorant have no argument. O brother of the people of Egypt, understand me, we never doubt Allah.'"

"'Do you not see the sun and the moon, the night and the day? They enter and never get confused, and they return. They are compelled; they have no place except their own place. If they were able to leave, why would they return?'"

quotes.caption: Ali ibn Abi Talib, in al-Amili, Wasa'il al-Shia, vol.1, p.418

paragraphs.text: فإني لجالس إذ ورد علي أمير المؤمنين ﵇ فقال : يا أخا الأزد ، معك طهور ؟ قلت : نعم ، فناولته الإداوة
"I was sitting when the Commander of the Faithful came to me and said, 'O brother of al-Azd, do you have water for purification?' I said, 'Yes,' and handed him the waterskin."

quotes.caption: Imam al-Sadiq, in al-Amili, Wasa'il al-Shia, vol.10, p.351

paragraphs.text: فقال له أبو عبد الله ﵇ : أفلا أزيدك من فضله فضلا يا أخا اليمن ؟ قال : زدني يا ابن رسول الله
"Imam al-Sadiq said to him, 'Shall I not add to you, of His bounty, an increase, O brother of Yemen?' He said, 'Increase it for me, son of the Messenger of Allah.'"

quotes.caption: The Prophet Muhammad, in al-Saduq, Man la Yahduruh al-Faqih, vol.2, p.202

paragraphs.text: فقال النبي ﵌ : أما أنت يا أخا الأنصار فإنك من قوم يؤثرون على أنفسهم وأنت قروي وهذا الثقفي بدوي أفتؤثره بالمسألة ؟
قال : نعم ، قال : أما أنت يا أخا ثقيف فإنك جئت تسألني عن وضوئك وصلاتك

"The Prophet said, 'As for you, O brother of the Ansar, you are of a people who give others preference over themselves. You are a townsman, and this man of Thaqif is a Bedouin. Will you give him preference in the asking?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'As for you, O brother of Thaqif, you have come to ask me about your ablution and your prayer.'"

quotes.caption: The Prophet Muhammad, al-Kulayni, al-Kafi (Dar al-Hadith ed.), vol.11, p.312

paragraphs.text: يَا أُخْتَ الْأَنْصَارِ ، جَزَاكُمُ اللَّهُ عَنْ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ خَيْراً ، فَقَدْ نَصَرَنِي رِجَالُكُمْ ، وَرَغِبَتْ (4) فِيَّ نِسَاؤُكُمْ
"O sister of the Ansar, may Allah reward you well on behalf of the Messenger of Allah. Your men have supported me, and your women have inclined to me."

quotes.caption: The Gospel of Matthew 1:1; Greek, Elzevir Textus Receptus; English, King James Version

paragraphs.text: βιβλος γενεσεως ιησου χριστου υιου δαβιδ υιου αβρααμ
Biblos geneseōs Iēsou Christou huiou Dauid huiou Abraam
"The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham."
